items.prompt: Choose the correct ending. If you heat ice, ___

options.text: it froze.
options.why: Froze is the past tense of freeze, the opposite of melting.

options.text: it would have melted.
options.why: This is for a past situation that did not happen.

options.text: it melts.
it melting.
options.why: Melting needs a helping verb, so this is not a complete sentence.

hints: This sentence is about something that is always true.
For facts that are always true, both parts of the sentence use the present tense.
Ask: what always happens to ice when it is heated?
items.explanation: If you heat ice, it melts. This is always true, so both clauses are in the present tense.

items.prompt: Write one word to complete the sentence. If it rains tomorrow, we ___ stay at home.
hints: The sentence is about something that could really happen tomorrow.
The if part is in the present tense. The result part talks about the future.
Which modal verb do we use for the future?
items.explanation: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home. For a real possibility in the future, use if with the present tense and will in the result.

items.prompt: Which sentence talks about something imaginary?

options.text: If I had wings, I would fly to school.
If it is sunny, we will go to the beach.
If you press this button, the light comes on.
options.why: This is a fact that is always true.

options.text: If the bus is late, we will walk.

hints: Imaginary means it cannot really happen, or is very unlikely.
Imaginary conditions use the past tense after if and would in the result.
Ask of each sentence: could this really happen?
items.explanation: People do not have wings, so this is imaginary. It uses had after if and would in the result.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a conditional sentence.
hints: Look for the word with a capital letter and the word with a full stop.
The if clause comes first, and it ends with a comma.
Start with If, then say who does the action.
items.explanation: If you water the plant, it will grow. The if clause comes first, then a comma, then the result.

items.prompt: Match each if clause to the ending that fits best.
pairs: If you mix red and yellow,
I will give him your message.
I would fly over the volcano.
we would have caught the train.
hints: Each if clause needs a result in the matching tense.
Present goes with present or will. Past goes with would. Had left goes with would have.
Start with If you mix red and yellow. Is that always true?
items.explanation: Facts use the present tense, real future possibilities use will, imaginary situations use would, and past situations that did not happen use would have.

items.prompt: Write the correct form of be. If I ___ you, I would wear a coat.
hints: This is an imaginary situation: I cannot really be you.
In imaginary if sentences, formal English uses a special form of be.
It is the same form you would use with they or we in the past.
items.explanation: In imaginary situations, we say If I were you. This is how we give advice politely.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence. If Pak Budi had checked the weather, he ___ his umbrella.

options.text: will take
options.why: Will take is for real future possibilities.

options.text: would take
options.why: This is for imaginary present situations. Had checked tells us it is about the past.

options.text: would have taken
takes

hints: Had checked tells us the sentence is about the past.
For a past situation that did not happen, the result uses would have and a past participle.
Did Pak Budi check the weather? Then did he take his umbrella?
items.explanation: He did not check the weather, so he did not take his umbrella. Past situations that did not happen use had in the if clause and would have in the result.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences that are correct.

options.text: If the road floods, the school will close.
If I would have known, I would have helped.
options.why: After if, use had known, not would have known.

options.text: If she had studied, she would have passed.
If you will mix blue and yellow, you get green.
options.why: For a fact, use the present tense after if: If you mix.

options.text: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

hints: Check the verb straight after if or unless in each sentence.
Would and will do not usually come straight after if.
Start with the sentence about the road. Is it a real possibility with the right tenses?
items.explanation: The correct sentences use the present after if for real possibilities, and had studied with would have passed for the past.

items.prompt: What does this sentence tell us? If we had planted the seeds in March, we would have had tomatoes by now.

options.text: They planted the seeds in March and have tomatoes now.
options.why: Had planted in an if clause means it did not happen.

options.text: They will plant the seeds next March.
options.why: The sentence is about the past, not the future.

options.text: They do not like tomatoes.
options.why: The sentence does not tell us what they like.

options.text: They did not plant the seeds in March, so they have no tomatoes yet.

hints: This kind of conditional talks about the past.
If clauses with had describe something that did not happen.
Ask: did they plant the seeds in March?
items.explanation: The sentence imagines a different past. They did not plant the seeds in March, so they do not have tomatoes yet.

items.prompt: Which sentence means the same as this one? You won’t pass the test unless you revise.

options.text: If you revise, you won’t pass the test.
options.why: This means revising would stop you passing.

options.text: If you don’t revise, you won’t pass the test.
You will pass the test if you don’t revise.
Unless you don’t revise, you will pass the test.
options.why: This double negative makes the meaning confusing.

hints: Unless means if not.
Replace unless with if not and see what the sentence becomes.
Start with: You won’t pass the test if you...
items.explanation: Unless means if not, so the sentence means: If you don’t revise, you won’t pass the test.
